snippet.title: i wired my toilet to a Raspberry Pi
snippet.description:
Companies still have to ship AI, and their AI agents now have real access to real servers and real data. Wiz gives you the complete context and runtime protection to adopt AI fast and safely. See Wiz AIDR in action with a demo and tell them Chuck sent you: https://ntck.co/WizAIDR


My toilet officially has an IP address. Every time my editors flush, all of our computers drop off the NAS and even the internet kind of hiccups, so I put a float switch in the toilet tank and wired it to an old Raspberry Pi. Now I know exactly when that toilet flushes, down to the millisecond, and my whole team gets a Slack alert. It took a Lego, a few tries, a few zip ties and way too much hand washing. That's just good IT work. In this video you'll learn how a float switch works (two metal strips, a glass tube and a magnet), how to wire one to the GPIO pins on a Raspberry Pi, why the Pi's built-in pull-up resistor keeps stray electrical noise from faking a flush, and how a small Python script checks the pin every tenth of a second and logs every flush to a JSON file. Whether you have never touched a GPIO pin or everything in your house already has an IP address, this is a very dumb project with a real IT lesson inside it: when something weird happens on your network, log everything around it.

snippet.title: your house needs TWO networks (here's why)
snippet.description:
Try Flare for free: https://ntck.co/flare-opnsense

Your smart fridge could be the way a hacker gets into your home network. So in part two of Mike's network build, I use OPNsense and VLANs to split his one flat network into separate networks for work, users, and a quarantined IoT network that can't touch anything else. The firewall is the mini PC from Japan we built in part one, the switch is a QNAP I'd never used (it has a dent), and DHCP almost broke me over one hidden checkbox. Then I told Mike his IoT devices were finally locked down, and he asked me what an IoT device is.

In this video you'll learn what a VLAN actually is and how to create one in OPNsense, how trunk (tagged) and untagged ports work on a managed switch, how to give each new network its own gateway IP and DHCP range (plus the one DHCP setting Claude Code had to find for me), how deny-by-default firewall rules and an alias keep your IoT devices locked in their own corner, and what happens when you point an AI agent (Pig, running Hermes on a Raspberry Pi) at a switch with no CLI. Whether you've never heard the word VLAN or you already built the OPNsense box from part one, this is how you turn one network into as many as you need.

Apple says the new M5 Ultra Mac Studio is up to 4x faster than the M3 Ultra at LLM prompt processing. I own an M3 Ultra Mac Studio, so I raced them head to head on local AI: same model, same prompt, same settings. On a 32,000-token prompt with Qwen3.8 27B, the M5 Ultra started answering in 21.7 seconds. The M3 Ultra took 82.8. That's 3.8x. Then the M5 wrote the answer 1.5x faster (43.3 vs 28.1 tokens per second), which lines up with its jump in memory bandwidth from 819 GB/s to 1.2 TB/s.

Then I threw my real work at it. Whisper transcribed two hours of my audio in about a minute and a half. A local vision model described my footage, a job I pay the Gemini video API for right now. I generated images with FLUX.2 and video with LTX-2.5, ran my Hermes agent on a local model, tried an open decision model (Laya) in place of Jev, and let a local model edit a video in DaVinci Resolve through its MCP server. All of it runs on the Mac. No internet required.

In this video you'll learn how the M5 Ultra and M3 Ultra compare for running LLMs locally with MLX, why the wait for the first word (time to first token) got about 4x shorter while writing speed only got 1.5x faster, how model size and dense vs mixture-of-experts models change the numbers, and whether a Mac Studio makes sense as your own local AI server.

Apple loaned me the M5 Ultra Mac Studio for this video, and it goes back to them. They don't control what I say, and all the tests and all the numbers are mine.

snippet.title: this Raspberry Pi belongs on your wall
snippet.description:
This video is sponsored by NetworkChuck Coffee. Grab a bag of Default Route (my favorite) and fuel your next build: https://ntck.co/coffee

Raspberry Pi sent me the new Raspberry Pi Touch Display 2, the 10 inch portrait version, and I mounted it on my studio wall to run all my Home Assistant and homelab stuff. It is a gorgeous little screen (1200x1920, real IPS, 10 finger touch, 400 nits) and at $80 it is a steal. There is one catch though, and a lot of you are not going to like it: this thing only works on the Raspberry Pi 5 and the Compute Modules. Your Pi 3 or Pi 4 will not work at all.

In this video I unbox it, walk through everything that is new versus the old touch display, hit a wall when it powered on and did absolutely nothing (turns out you have to update the firmware on your Pi 5, the EEPROM, before it will recognize the screen), mount it with nothing but a drill and some screws, and finally turn it into a beautiful Home Assistant dashboard using an open source kiosk app called TouchKio. Whether you are building a smart home wall panel, a homelab status board, or you just want your Raspberry Pi to show off what it is doing, this is a really good option.

snippet.title: Fable 5 is back.....run these prompts before July 12th
snippet.description:
Fable 5 — the most powerful AI on earth — got pulled offline by the U.S. government three days after it launched, and it just came back. But for most of us the free window is only a handful of days (through July 7). So I sat down with Daniel Miessler, who's already living inside that window, to figure out the one thing that actually matters: what's worth asking it before it's gone.
